title: Telling It Like It Happened
blurb: Tell and react to a story

steps.html:
Two people tell two disasters. One woke up in a school playground. The other spent nine hours in an airport and got her luggage back a day late. Then a film about a holiday that went right.

  • Follow two spoken stories and catch the order of events
  • Recognise the phrases English uses to react to a story
  • Watch a documentary about a learning holiday
  • Write an email of complaint that asks for something specific

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: Sabrina's account moves from the lorry, to the coach, to the missed connection, to what she did next.
steps.prompt: Why does she tell it in that order rather than starting with the outcome?
options: Because she cannot remember the outcome clearly enough to open with it.
Because each step explains the next, so the listener reaches her decision already understanding why she had no alternative.
Because the interviewer asked her to give the events in that order.
steps.answer: Because each step explains the next, so the listener reaches her decision already understanding why she had no alternative.
steps.why: A narrative in cause order defends the decision at the end of it. Starting with the outcome would invite the question she is answering.

steps.title: Which tense, and why it changes the meaning
steps.html:
Both stories run on the contrast. This stage is about choosing between them under pressure.

Spoken stories move fast, and the two tenses do different jobs at speed. The past simple is the next thing that happened. The past perfect is the explanation for it, dropped in from earlier.

Listen to Sabrina: we got stuck in a traffic jam (past simple — the event) … apparently there'd been an accident, a lorry had turned over (past perfect — why). The explanation is always older than the event it explains.

The contrast can change the meaning completely. When I arrived, the flight was cancelled — I was there when they cancelled it. When I arrived, the flight had been cancelled — they had cancelled it before I got there.

In speech the past perfect is usually contracted — we'd been camping, I'd parked, there'd been an accident — which is why it can be hard to hear. Listen for the 'd and for the past participle after it.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from the two recordings.

We 'd been camping in the south of France.
Before the story's moment. Past perfect continuous, contracted.

We 'd booked into a campsite outside Paris.
Also earlier. Contracted had.

We reached the suburbs at about three in the morning.
On the line. Past simple.

She threw the map at me and fell asleep.
Two events in order.

You know what I 'd done? I 'd parked in a school playground.
The explanation, from earlier.

We got stuck in a traffic jam.
On the line.

Apparently there 'd been an accident — a lorry had turned over.
Both older than the jam.

The flight had been cancelled.
Past perfect passive: it happened before she reached the lounge.

I had to wait nine hours.
Had to is past simple obligation, not past perfect.

They lost my luggage. Just for a day.
Past simple — the last event in the sequence.

steps.title: Choosing the tense that says what you mean
steps.html:
1. The facts: at 11:40 the airline cancelled the flight. At 11:55 Sabrina reached the departure lounge.
  2. You are telling the story from her arrival, so reached is past simple: I ran through to the departure lounge.
  3. The cancellation is older than that arrival, so it steps back into the past perfect: The flight had been cancelled.
  4. Check the meaning. The flight was cancelled when I arrived would suggest she watched it happen — which is not the story.
  5. Note the passive: she does not say who cancelled it, because it does not matter. Had been + past participle.

steps.title: Write your email of complaint.
steps.sub: 160–190 words. Something went wrong on a journey or a course you booked. Set out what happened, in order, and ask for one specific thing.
steps.html:
• Open with what you are complaining about, and any reference number.
  • Set out what happened, in order, in the past simple.
  • Use the past perfect for anything that had already happened before you got there.
  • Say clearly what the consequence was for you.
  • Ask for one specific thing, then close formally.

Useful language

  • I am writing to complain about …
  • By the time I reached … , the … had already been …
  • I had booked … on the understanding that …
  • This was extremely inconvenient because …
  • I am therefore writing to request compensation for …
  • I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, …
steps.modelHtml:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about my journey from Karagandy to Almaty on 14 May, booking reference KZ-4471.

The coach left forty minutes late. A lorry had turned over on the road ahead, and although that was clearly not the company's fault, no member of staff told us anything for over an hour. By the time we reached the terminal, my connecting service had already left.

I had booked the two journeys together, on the understanding that a connection would be held. Nobody at the desk was able to explain why it had not been. I spent the night in the terminal and reached Almaty eleven hours later than planned, which meant I missed the first day of a course I had paid for in full.

I am therefore writing to request compensation for the course fee and for the cost of the replacement ticket. I have attached both receipts.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours faithfully,
A. Ivanova
